Kaiser Permanente Issues Embarrassingly Stupid Press Release
On Marijuana And Teens With STDs

(Marijuananews note: First, notice their headline. Marijuana is the first word. This guarantees coverage by the prohibitionist media. It will also qualify them for a NIDA grant.

Second, notice also that there is absolutely no mention of alcohol, even though it is much more widely used than marijuana.

Third, correlation is not causation, and there is no way that marijuana use could "cause" a sexually transmitted disease, at least not without ruining your bong.

According to the data presented here, weekly marijuana use correlates with a higher rate of STDs. Does this mean that marijuana is actually a "risk factor?"

Well, certainly getting stoned is not likely to make a teenager more sexually cautious, but this is not at all the same thing as being a cause of an STD.

For example, teens who are "risk takers" may be more likely to use marijuana and have sex with older partners. Teens who are unhappy and who use marijuana to self-medicate, may also lack the self-esteem to take proper care of themselves. Teens who want to have sex with older partners may use marijuana more, or older men may use marijuana to seduce teens. There are a number of scenarios that would explain this correlation, but this press release mentions none.

It will be interesting to see how much media coverage this gets.)

OAKLAND, Calif.--(BW HealthWire)—

Aug. 12, 1999--

African American teenagers and young women who have older sex partners are 3 times more likely to get a sexually transmitted disease (STD), according to a study published in Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine by researchers at the University of California San Francisco and Kaiser Permanente’s Division of Research.

The risk of getting an STD is also doubled for those who smoke marijuana once a week.

"Healthcare providers who work with adolescents and young adults should be aware of these findings and talk with their younger patients," says lead author Cherrie Boyer, Ph.D. "And young women need to be aware of the factors that put them more at risk of contracting these diseases."

The study involved 285 young men and women who came to a Kaiser Permanente teen clinic. The 13 to 21-year-olds generally attended the clinic for reproductive health care.

"Many of these young women and men knowingly take chances,"

Older sex partners may increase a teen’s risk of STDs because the partner is more sexually experienced. The authors also found that the risk-taking behaviors of African-American teenagers were no different from the other groups surveyed and concluded that the teens’ sexual partners, again, may account for the higher rate of STDs.

49% of all the teens surveyed had had sex with 2 or more partners within the 9 months prior to the study, 43% had had sex with a new partner, and nearly 65% thought their sexual partner had had sex with someone other than themselves. 72% of the study’s participants admitted their use of condoms was "inconsistent," even when their behavior put them at risk.

44% of the teens in the study reported using marijuana at least once a month, and the rate was higher among those who’d been diagnosed with an STD (55%).

"These findings strongly suggest that the use of illicit substances, especially marijuana, plays a role in risk and acquisition of STDs for young persons," say the authors.

(Marijuananews note: Especially marijuana? Does this mean that there is a lower risk in using heroin or cocaine? If so, why?

And what about alcohol use? Remember Ogden Nash’s line: "Candy’s dandy, but liquor’s quicker.")

See

"It is possible that addressing substance use behavior in young persons may influence their decision-making processes and ultimately the behaviors that place them at risk for STDs."

(Marijuananews note: What a great idea! Let’s start a national prohibitionist propaganda campaign against marijuana, then we won’t have these problems with teen sex.

They must have had a NIDA grant!)

Previous studies of sexually transmitted diseases and their victims have shown that 12 million cases of STDs are reported every year in the U.S. 25% of those cases occur among teenagers 15 to 19 years old. The most prevalent reported STD is Chlamydia trachomatis, which accounts for about 4 million cases of sexually transmitted disease in the U.S. each year.

Dr. Chuck Wibbelsman is a pediatrician and researcher with Kaiser Permanente in Northern California. Dr. Cherrie Boyer is a health psychology researcher and associate professor at the University of California San Francisco, in its Division of Adolescent Medicine.

Co-authors are Mary-Ann Shafer, M.D., professor of pediatrics and associate director of the division of adolescent medicine at UCSF; Eileen Teitle, N.P., pediatric nurse practitioner with Kaiser Permanente Medical Center, San Francisco; Donald A. Seeberg, B.A., research associate at UCSF and Julius Schachter, PhD, professor of laboratory medicine at UCSF.

UCSF is recognized as one of the leading patient care, biomedical research and graduate education centers in the world.

Kaiser Permanente is America’s leading non-profit integrated health care organization. Founded in 1945, it is a group-practice prepayment program with headquarters in Oakland. Kaiser Permanente serves the health care needs of 8.6 million members in 17 states and the District of Columbia.

Today, it encompasses Kaiser Foundation Health Plan Inc. and subsidiaries, Kaiser Foundation Hospitals, and the Permanente Medical Groups, as well as an affiliation with Group Health Cooperative, based in Seattle. Nationwide, Kaiser Permanente includes about 90,000 technical, administrative and clerical employees and about 10,000 physicians representing all specialties.
